1.title: Tool Interfaces and Structured Error Responses
1.text: Welcome to Module five: Tool Interfaces and Structured Error Responses. This module covers task statements two point one and two point two: tool interfaces and structured error responses. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Why the tool description is the main thing Claude uses to pick a tool. What a good description contains, and how to fix overlapping tools. The M C P (Model Context Protocol) is Error pattern and structured error metadata. Error categories, retryable versus non-retryable, and access failure versus valid empty result.

1.title: Case Check-In: Birchwood Supply's Agent Picks the Wrong Tool
1.text: Our running case is Birchwood Supply. Birchwood Supply's Agent Picks the Wrong Tool. Customers write: "is the blue kettle, item K-two thousand two hundred ten, in stock?". The agent keeps calling find product instead of check stock. Both tools are described in three words ("Finds product information", "Gets stock details") and take similar identifiers.

1.title: Tool Descriptions Drive Tool Selection
1.text: Tool Descriptions Drive Tool Selection. Claude decides which tool to call mainly from the tool's name, description and input schema. Minimal descriptions leave it guessing between similar tools. A strong description states: what it does, expected input formats, example queries it should handle, edge cases and boundaries ("use this for X, not for Y: use check stock for availability").

1.title: Tool Descriptions Drive Tool Selection, continued
1.text: Tool Descriptions Drive Tool Selection, continued. The figure shows this: A good tool description: purpose, input formats, examples, edge cases and boundaries against similar tools.

1.title: Tool Descriptions Drive Tool Selection, continued
1.text: Tool Descriptions Drive Tool Selection, continued. check stock: "Gets stock details". check stock: "Returns units on hand and the restock date for O N E item. Input: an item code like K-two thousand two hundred ten (letter, dash, four digits). Use for availability questions. Do not use to search by name or description: use find product for that. Returns not found if the code does not exist.".

1.title: Fixing overlap
1.text: Fixing overlap. Ambiguous or overlapping descriptions cause misrouting (two tools such as analyze content and analyze document with near-identical text). Rename and rewrite to remove the overlap: analyze content to extract web results, with a web-specific description. Split a generic tool into purpose-specific tools with defined input and output contracts: analyze document to extract data points, summarize content, verify claim against source. Check the system prompt for keyword-sensitive wording that can override good descriptions and create unintended tool associations (for example, a line that says "when the user mentions an item, always call find product"). Exam tip: "Most effective first step" for wrong tool choice between similar tools to expand the descriptions (formats, examples, edge cases, boundaries). Few-shot examples (extra tokens), a pre-routing layer (over-engineered) and merging the tools (more effort) are not the first step.

1.title: Fixing overlap, continued
1.text: Fixing overlap, continued. Exam tip: Ambiguous or overlapping descriptions cause misrouting: rename, split into purpose-specific tools or rewrite them, and check the system prompt for keyword traps.

1.title: Structured Error Responses
1.text: Structured Error Responses. An M C P tool signals failure with the is Error flag on its result so the agent knows the call failed; the content should say why, in a form the agent can act on.

1.title: Structured Error Responses, continued
1.text: Structured Error Responses, continued. Transient. Examples: Timeout, service unavailable. Retry?: Yes (with backoff). What the agent should do: Retry, then try an alternative or report partial results. Validation. Examples: Bad input format, missing field. Retry?: After fixing the input. What the agent should do: Correct the argument and call again. Business (policy). Examples: Refund window expired, limit exceeded. Retry?: No (retriable: false). What the agent should do: Explain to the customer in plain words, or escalate. Permission. Examples: Not allowed to access this record. Retry?: No (unless access changes). What the agent should do: Stop and escalate or ask for authorization.

1.title: Structured Error Responses, continued
1.text: Structured Error Responses, continued. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Structured Error Responses, continued
1.text: Structured Error Responses, continued. The figure shows this: Error categories and the right response: retry transient errors, fix validation errors, explain business errors, escalate permission errors. Why generic errors hurt: a plain "Operation failed" hides whether to retry, fix the input, or stop. The agent wastes retries or gives up too early. Structured metadata (error Category, is Retryable, a human-readable description) lets the agent choose the right recovery, and prevents wasted retry attempts.

1.title: Structured Error Responses, continued
1.text: Structured Error Responses, continued. For business rule violations include retriable: false and a customer-friendly explanation the agent can pass on. Local recovery first: a subagent should retry transient failures itself and propagate to the coordinator only what it cannot resolve, together with partial results and what was attempted (Module thirteen).

1.title: Access failure versus valid empty result
1.text: Access failure versus valid empty result. Meaning. Access failure: The query could not be completed (timeout, auth). Valid empty result: The query ran fine and found no matches. Signal. Access failure: is Error: true with category. Valid empty result: Success with an empty list. Agent behavior. Access failure: Decide: retry, alternative, partial. Valid empty result: Report "nothing found" as a real answer.

1.title: Access failure versus valid empty result, continued
1.text: Access failure versus valid empty result, continued. The figure shows this: Do not confuse the two: an error means the answer is unknown; an empty success means the answer is none. Exam tip: Returning an empty result as success when a timeout happened is an anti-pattern: the agent will conclude that nothing exists.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Selection signal: The tool description (plus name and schema) is the primary mechanism. Good description: Purpose, input formats, example queries, edge cases, boundaries versus similar tools. Overlap fixes: Rename plus rewrite; split generic tools; check system prompt for keyword-sensitive wording. First step: Better descriptions before few-shot, routers or merging. Error flag: M C P is Error (A P I: is error in tool result). Categories: Transient (retry), validation (fix input), business (retriable:false, friendly text), permission. Metadata: error Category, is Retryable, human-readable description. Empty versus failure: Access failure equals error; no matches equals valid empty success. Local recovery: Subagent retries transient errors; propagates only the unresolved, with partial results.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. The agent often calls find product when shoppers ask whether an item code is in stock, instead of check stock. Both tools have one-line descriptions and accept similar identifiers. What is the most effective first step? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Descriptions are the primary selection mechanism, so improving them is the low-effort, high-leverage fix. The other options add tokens, infrastructure or redesign work before the root cause is addressed.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Two tools, analyze content and analyze document, have nearly identical descriptions and are often confused. Which fix is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Renaming and rewriting removes the functional overlap that causes misrouting.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A generic analyze document tool is used for extraction, summaries and fact checks, with inconsistent results. How should it be redesigned? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Specific tools with clear contracts (for example extract data points, summarize content, verify claim against source) are easier for the model to select and use correctly.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Well-written tool descriptions exist, yet the agent keeps preferring one tool whenever the user says "item". The system prompt says: "When the user mentions an item, call find product first." What is the likely cause? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Review system prompts for wording that overrides tool descriptions.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A tool call fails with a timeout. Which tool result best supports recovery? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Structured metadata tells the agent that retrying makes sense. A generic message hides the choice, and an empty success would be treated as "no data".

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A refund request is rejected because the return window has closed. What should the tool return? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A policy violation is a business error that must not be retried; the explanation lets the agent communicate it well.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. A search tool returns zero matches for an existing customer's order history. How should the agent treat this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A successful query with no matches is a real answer; do not confuse it with failure.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. A subagent hits a brief network timeout on a search. What is the best behavior? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Resolve transient problems locally and escalate only what cannot be resolved, with context.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. Which field combination in an error result prevents wasted retries on a permission failure? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Category and retryable flag let the agent stop retrying and escalate instead.

2.title: Practice Question 10
2.text: Question ten. Select two. Which two changes most improve selection between two similar tools? The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and E. Clear formats, examples and boundaries differentiate tools. Removing text, meaningless names and generic errors make selection and recovery harder.

2.title: Practice Question 11
2.text: Question eleven. Select two. Which two pieces of metadata should a failed tool call return to guide recovery? The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and D. A category and a retryable flag tell the agent whether to retry, fix the input or stop. The other items do not support a recovery decision.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all eleven answers. Question one: A. Question two: C. Question three: C. Question four: D. Question five: D. Question six: A. Question seven: C. Question eight: B. Question nine: D. Question ten: C and E. Question eleven: C and D. In the next module, we continue the course.
